. Mr. D. D. McKENZIB (Cape Breton North): Mr. 'Speaker, I hold in my hand the newspaper called the Financial Post, which was the subject of a good deal of discussion this afternoon. On the front page of this newspaper I notice a conspicuous headline which says:
"Evils in the army arising out of the liquor traffic. Millions lost to Canada. Wet canteen is ruining countless Canadian soldiers. Vice rampant as result of liquor obtainable in the army. How this affects Canada in dollars and cents, adding to our heavy burden of debt."
No doubt it was the conspicuous, glaring headline that caught the eye of the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) and led him to read the lengthy and striking article of which that is the heading. As an hon. gentleman who is interested in the affairs of this country and of the Canadian army and of the Empire, and anxious for their welfare in every phase and ramification, he was no doubt led to inquire as to the truth or falsity of,this article. It is not long since an article appeared in a newspaper no more conspicuous, and not regarded as any greater authority than the Post, having something to do with a criticism in connection with the Ross rifle. That paper was taken up by one of the ministers of the Crown and made the subject of comment in this House; that minister even -went so far as to intimate that any person who would give publicity to such language should be shot. The article in the Post to which reference has been made appeared on the 21st of the month. To-day is the 26th .so there has been ample opportunity for ministers to notice this article and reply to or refute it; but nothing of the kind was done. The hon. member for Rouville refrained for five days from making any comments on- this article, I suppose expecting a satisfactory reply to it to be made by some one on behalf of the Government, an explanation that would be satisfactory to the people of this country, particularly to those who have sons in the army or expecting to go overseas. Nothing had been said and. so it was quite proper for an hon. gentleman of the prominence and responsibility of the hon. member for Rouville to bring this matter up in the House, and make some inquiries about it. I do not think it was at all necessary for the hon. gentlemen opposite to fly into such a passion as they did on account of this inquiry. All that was necessary was

for the Minister of Militia to say that the article was not true, and to give such explanation as would be fitting from the parliamentary head of the military service of Canada. But I am sorry to say that occasion has been taken by the forelock and by some of our safety-first colonels in this House to spread themselves and to give the country to understand that they had special and first-hand knowledge about this thing. We never heard of them very much before and I do not blame them for taking this opportunity of making it known to the people that they did don the khaki and did go across the Atlantic, otherwise we would perhaps never have heard about them. There was no occasion to fly into a passion as they did in giving this explanation. One hon. gentleman, who sits on that side of the House and who donned the khaki and who went across the ocean just as well as the colonels who have spoken so strongly to-day, gave much more damaging information in respect to what is afflicting our young men on the other side of the water than the mere inquiry which was instituted by the hon. member for Rouville. I am sure that if any one should be subject to criticism, if any one is deserving of condemnation for making statements in connection with the evils into which our young men fall in connection with the army, it is this gentleman on the other side who is just as well informed, I presume, as any of those who have spoken to-day. He has given most startling information. But they say nothing about him, he is all right. But any hon. gentleman from this side of the House who says anything at all about any matter calling for criticism is made the subject of attack. We in this Parliament profess to be proud to follow the practices of the Mother of Parliaments in the great mother country, and if we do so in parliamentary matters I do not think we shall go far astray. What has been the course of criticism in the Mother of Parliaments since war broke out. It will not be denied that at the outbreak of the war they had in England as strong a Government as they ever had in that country. It was led by as able a man as ever occupied the high position of First Minister in Great Britain. What has happened? Criticism has practically driven that Government out of power and has forced that premier to give up the full power which he enjoyed and to enter into an alliance with the Opposition and to form a compromise coalition Government. This great leader in England was obliged to vacate

his high position at the head of the Government and the country and give way to another man. We would he safe in following the high example of the Mother of Parliaments. Therefore I submit that no man has the right to come here and censure us for any action we may take in bringing matters before the House in a public way if it be found necessary to do so. When did the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) become so opposed to publicity? He used to be a strong man on publicity. He used to be much in favour of seeing things brought to the full blaze of the light of public opinion, so far at least as the public press and Parliament could do so. I remember well, as I was here some years before that hon. member came to this House, when he published in a newspaper of his- own party, possibly his own organ in the province of Manitoba, a full report of a speech that he never .delivered in this House; .and, what is even more extraordinary, he also published in the same newspaper the reply that Mr. Oliver made to it- which was never delivered in the House either. These were the old-time practices of my hon. friend. I am surprised that he should now turn his hose on publicity with such force and disapprove so severely of the course taken by the hon. member for Rou-ville in bringing this matter to the notice of the House. If the speech of the member for Rouville is published in the newspapers it will he very different from the publicity of the hon. member for Selkirk, fOT it will be a speech which was actually delivered in this House. My hon. friend used to be perfectly satisfied with speeches which he himself wrote down and sent to the press. He also took the extraordinary course of making and publishing the other fellow's speech as wall.

We were told by hon. gentlemen opposite, particularly by that preacher of righteousness, the Minister of Finance, that it was scandalous, shameful, preposterous, cowardly; it was had in all the .adjectives that Webster, Worcester, or Walker could produce, that this matter should he brought to the attention of the House. The preacher who stands in the pulpit and advises the ungodly man to forsake hi-s -ways and to return unto the Lord, is, according to hon. gentlemen opposite, insulting and scandalizing his people. He is accusing them of being traitors .and cowards if ha points out to them the way in which they ought to go and urges them to avoid every appearance of evil. According to the doctrine of hon. gentlemen opposite, preachers must now toe informed that they should no longer .advise their people to .seek first the Kingdom of God and His righteousness and that then all other things shall be added unto them. Neither Parliament nor press hesitated to discuss these things. Hon. gentlemen cannot escape responsibility for the wet canteen, if it is a bad thing. We have jurisdiction over there in the person of a minister of the Crown representing this Government, who has full sway over military men while they are in our own camps. If it is a good thing that we should have a dry canteen in Canada-and I am in favour of it-why should we not have a dry canteen on the other side? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret exceedingly that the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has introduced here to-day a discussion that can serve no useful purpose, and I feel satisfied, when the news goes abroad throughout Canada to-morrow, as it undoubtedly will, that notwithstanding the time of stress in which we are living, when minutes mean so much, the House of Commons of the Dominion of Canada has devoted a whole day to the discussion of a subject on the strength of an article of doubtful quality that appears in a newspaper, many of the friends of the youths who are to-day fighting the battles of the Empire will suffer untold anxieties and alarm with regard to those who are near and dear to them. We have listened to the speech of the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), who has not advanced any arguments to sustain the newspaper article which has been read here this afternoon, but who has endeavoured to justify the attitude of hon. gentlemen on the opposite side of the House who' have spoken on this question. We heard from the lips of the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) the statement that the whole question was whether there should be a dry canteen or a wet canteen, and that we were justified in discussing that question. Yet, the leader of the Opposition, the hon. gentleman who has moved the motion and those who have supported him, have taken no stand in regard to what the hon. member for West Lamb-ton has said, that the question before the House is whether there should be a dry canteen or a wet canteen; they do not commit themselves either one way or the other upon that question. I must, therefore, ask myself what object they have in view in introducing this question into this House at this particular time? We are living in one of the most critical, most strenuous ages that have ever confronted the people of this world, when the people of the British Empire are bending every sinew, exerting every energy to win in the greatest conflict that has ever engaged the attention of man. We have sent overseas many thousands of the flower of the manhood of Canada-we have not sent them;

they have gone voluntarily. Hon. members will remember that a large proportion of the First Contingent consisted of men who were borti and who grew up in the old land, men who had been in this country for only a few years. Yet hon. gentlemen in this House insult the Government of the British Empire, the Government that are endeavouring, aye, that have made good progress, towards winning this war for civilization, for liberty and for mankind. They are the people that you are condemning by your action to-day.
It is not the Government of Canada but the Government of the British Empire that you are condemning, and as I said before this discussion cannot possibly serve any useful purpose; indeed, I believe it will do a great injury to the cause that we all ought to have so much at heart. Some of us know intimately many of the young men who went over with the first contingent, and day after day we have followed their fortunes with the utmost interest, and when we have it from the lips of these men themselves that there is not the danger that has been suggested here today, I would ask the members of this House what can be the object of a man of the prominence of the hon. member from Rouville, a man who occupied a prominent position in the late government, in introducing a question in this House about the authenticity of which he himself is not satisfied, his information being derived from a mere newspaper article. The hon. member from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) holds the paper up and says it was no douibt the glaring headlines that induced the hon. member to bring this matter before the House. The hon. member for Rouville is not a youth in polities; he understands the meaning of words, and I again say what I have said before, that I believe many of the statements that have been made and published by the leaders of the Liberal party and by the Liberal press have done much to retard recruiting in Canada. I believe that when the discussion that has taken place here to-day is spread broadcast throughout the country, recruiting in Canada will be injured once more. In view of the statements that have been made by hon. gentlemen opposite and by one hon. member on this side of the House, the hon. member from Peterborough (Mr. Burnham), I think we should be doing a good 'act if we agreed to expunge from the records of this House the whole discussion on this miserable question that has taken place this afternoon. We are

living in a strenuous age, an age calling on each of us to do his utmost; and yet, can any man who has listened to this discussion conceal from himself the fact that some members of this House have endeavoured to make political capital out of this miserable question? I am not here to make any apology for the men at the front. They need no apology from anyone in this House; they need no advice from any member of this House. They are able to take care of themselves, and able to advise us. When you think of what they have accomplished, can you have any doubt in your mind as to their being physically fit and able to cope with the pick of the enemy troops? When you think of the battles of Ypres, and of the capture of Vimy Ridge only a few days ago, everyone must realize that there cannot be the danger that has been implied here this afternoon.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have criticised hon. gentlemen on this side of the House who have raised battalions in this country and have taken them overseas. They have sneered at these patriotic men, who had the interests of their country at heart, and who would have liked to go to the front. These are the men who know what conditions are in England. I am not here to deprecate the value of the great work that has been done by the British Government. Our Allies are looking to the British Empire for every possible assistance. The British Government has been the backbone of the Allies, the brawn and sinew throughout the Whole conflict, and do you mean to tell me that we, sitting here thousands of miles from the scene of conflict, are in a position to criticise the British Government for lack of attention to their duties in respect of the fitness of the men they are sending to the front? Are these men crazy, are they fools, to allow men to be sent overseas unfit, when they are trying to raise men by every possible means? I can trust the British Government in this matter, a Government that has raised an army of nearly six million fighting men, and I am not going to sit in my seat and listen to hon. gentlemen opposite censuring the very best men the Empire can produce, men who are devoting every ounce of energy they possess towards winning the war. Nor would I be justified in sitting in my place and listening to hon. gentlemen opposite treating these subjects in a jocular way, and advancing arguments that are not pertinent to the question without raising a protest. Hon. gentlemen opposite know that this Gov-

eminent has absolutely nothing to do with these matters, and in view of the discussion here this afternoon I believe the people of Canada can come to no other conclusion than that the burdens of state rest very lightly upon some hon. members of this House when a whole day can be devoted to an aimless dischssion that can serve no useful purpose, and which I am sure the hon. member from Rouville now regrets that he ever introduced into this House. As I said before, I think we should expunge from the records the statements made not only by the hon. member for Rouville, but by the hon. member from Peterborough. They have made statements that are not justifiable, have slandered the men who are fighting our battles for us, men who realize their responsibilities better than hon. members sitting comfortably in this House. Some of those men have been in the thick of the fray for nearly three years, and thousands and, I am afraid, tens of thousands of them will never return to Canada The blood of those men that have fallen on the fields of France and Flanders is crying out to us to see that this fight is carried to a successful conclusion; and do you mean to tell me that a discussion of this nature is going to assist one iota in winning the war? It is much to our discredit that this question has been brought before the House and our time wasted, when there are so many other questions of importance demanding our attention.

Every one who ;is in a position to know knew that as long as there was liquor for sale in the City of Quebec, in the Province of Quebec, or the Dominion of Canada, too much of that liquor would find its way into Valcartier Camp. Nearly every night there was drinking in the tents around us-
This was in Valcartier with its dry canteen.
-and the following extracts from my diary speak for themselves.

Friday, September 13. Our tent pulled down by men returning drunk from Quebec. Lantern smashed; liberal dose of kerosene in the bread bag. R. B. staggering drunk, turned' somersault on the tent when it was down.
This in a dry canteen.
Tuesday, September 22. Tent ahead of us pulled down at midnight in the rain. Drunken brawl. In morning I counted outside the tent, seven empty gin bottles, four brandy flasks, one whiskey bottle and one Jamaica, rum.
All in a dry canteen. The hon. member for Rouville said that the whole question is whether there shall be a wet or a dry canteen, but here is this man's own description of a dry canteen.

What would a wet one
be?

This writer goes on to show that, notwithstanding the dry canteen, if you allow the manufacture, importation and sale of .liquor anywhere in the Dominion, it will not make much difference, for the men will get it if they want it. In the third column of the letter theTe is something also bearing out what I said as to his argument being in favour of total prohibition and not in favour of a dry canteen, his argument being that if liquor is manufactured nothing will prevent the soldier getting it if he wants it. He says:

Liquor in the army is bound up with the
question of liquor in the nation. "We cannot give up one and keep the other. As long as the manufacture and sale of liquor as a beverage remains unprohibited in Canada, Great Britain or France, so long will our armies be hampered in their struggle.
As in the army so in the nation, all attempts at "control" short of total prohibition are exasperating failures.
Dry canteens and all the rest of them.
The damage to war work caused by drunken civilians-
He does not confine his criticisms to drunken soldiers.
-will never be estimated, and who will say that all the guilt must be borne by the drunkard, not by the brewer and the distiller. The problem of compensation will be ready for discussion when the brewers and distillers come forward with a reasonable proposal of compensation by them for the criminal waste-
Then he goes on to discuss the problem of compensation. The argument of this writer, whoever he is, is not directed especially against the wet canteen, but is directed especially against the manufacture of liquor; and he says in substance and gives as evidence the conditions at Valcartier, that if it is manufactured and sold outside you will have the army drinking whiskey.
Life will not be safe, women and children will not be safe as long as we give the liquor traffic a free hand to turn madmen loose on society.
I might' read a whole column, it is a temperance lecture of the old kind in favour of the prohibition of the manufacture, importation and sale of intoxicating liquors.
The way this matter has been brought before the House, intentionally or otherwise, reflects upon the character of every officer, non-commissioned officer and man who has gone across the ocean to fight for the liberties of this country and is defamatory of every single one of them because the charges are made in a general way and applicable to every one; insulting to our soldiers, insulting to the men who are risking their lives for us, and many have sacri-fieed their lives and others wiHl do so while still others will come back crippled for life. And yet the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), on the strength of a letter like that, written by a man about whom he knows nothing, for the Financial Post does not pretend to know anything about him.

Yes, I read the whole thing; I did not stop at part of it as my hon. friend did. As I say, we have no evidence whatever as to who this man is, where he is from or what reliance is to be placed on his statements. I understood it to be said to-day that the hon. member, for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) desired to get some information touching this matter and went to the Minister of Militia quietly to ask him as to conditions across the sea. That, I submit, was a proper course to take.
I understood that the hon. member for Rou-ville (Mr. Lemieux) was requested to allow this motion to stand until the questions-asked the Minister of Militia by my hon. friend from Pictou should be answered. If these questions were answered and answered satisfactorily there would have been no necessity to bring this matter up here or anywhere else. It does not appear why the hon. member for Rouville did not wait instead of exposing every member of our expeditionary force to the insults that have been hurled against every one of them here this afternoon. These are men who are sacrificing their lives for this country. It is not fair treatment of our boys at the front. In addition to what I have already said we have, had the evidence here this afternoon of three or four hon. members of this House who have been on the ground and who know what the conditions are with respect to these particular charges. Not only that, out we have men commanding our men in France; we have men training our men in England, men who are on the ground. Does any one suppose that General Byng has no regard for the character or welfare of our young men over there? He is on the ground. He knows the conditions. I have confidence in General Byng and the Ganadian officers with him. Does any one believe for a moment that if conditions existed such as this man Goforth, wherever he comes from, said existed they would be permitted by these officers to continue? Does anyone for one moment believe that the gentlemen who represent the Government of Canada in England have no regard for the welfare of our young men over there? They have just as much regard for their welfare as any hon. gentleman on the other side of the
9 p.m. House or on this side of the House. I have confidence in those men who are on the ground. I think 53
we can safely leave the matter to them, although there is no objection to inquiring into it quietly. I submit that the hon. member for Rouville would have discharged his duties as an hon. member of this House better in the interests of this country and in fair play to the soldiers of this country if he had gone privately to the Minister of Militia and said: Here is a fellow called Goforth, I do not know where he comes from, who says something here in the shape of a letter which is not signed by him, which has no date, which I find in the Financial Post. There are some grave charges made in this letter. Can you tell me whether these conditions exist in England or not? If you cannot, will you be kind enough to ascertain by cable from somebody in England in whom you have confidence, who can tell you? Then he could wait a day or two until there was an opportunity to receive an answer, and if the answer was satisfactory he would have spared the relatives of these boys who are at the front from feeling that their sons and husbands and brothers have 'been insulted and defamed by several members of the Opposition in this House.

One would think, to hear the Minister of Labour talk, that we were in Russia before the revolution. Does he not know that every government of the Allies except the Canadian; Government has either turned itself inside out or been turned inside out by some other power since the war began, on account of criticism offered by serious men who had the interests of their country at heart just as much as those to whom their criticism was directed? The soldiers at the front are intelligent and are not to be fooled by such talk as the Minister of Labour indulged in to-day. They are sons of men in this House; they are sons of Canadian families, and any discussion regarding them should be entered into from an intelligent standpoint, not by a silly appeal to those who are fighting for us while we are at home. They understand just what a man means, no matter what he says, whether in this House or elsewhere. are now practically none. We have removed the temptation from the men in the Canadian camps. The ex-Minister of Militia established the principle of dry canteen

and where is he now? He is not in this Government, and I should judge from the remarks of the Minister of Labour that the Government had changed its mind on this dry canteen question. For my part, whether the Canadian Government or any other Government has control, I am absolutely in favour of the principle that there should be no wet canteen in the camps where our boys are located.

speechtext:
I want to differentiate; no one can accuse me of being an extremist. I have no sympathy with the idea entertained by some good-thinking people that we should not give our boys at the front cigarettes and that kind of thing. I am in favour of letting the men have anything that will comfort them without injuring them. But it cannot be for the benefit of our men in the training camps-I am applying my remarks solely to the training camps-that they should have wet canteens. The member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. McCurdy) pointed out a condition in England that did not exist here. It did exist here, until a few months ago, at Camp Niagara, Borden Camp, Toronto, London, Brockville, Ottawa-the very conditions that he outlined as now existing in England. Nothwithstanding that, the *Government of which he is a near member, established the principle of a dry canteen. If that principle 'be right so far as the training camps in Canada are concerned -and the Government is committed to the principle-surely lit would not be wrong to ask that the same principle be adopted and carried out when our boys go overseas.
As to the men in the firing line, some hon. gentlemen opposite have endeavoured to draw a red herring across the trail. No one is discussing what is done in the trenches. If the experienced officers in charge of the men on the firing line believe that under trying circumstances-the seriousness of which not a man in this House save one, perhaps, thoroughly understands-a certain ration each day or at certain periods should be given to the men, I am not going to say that they are wrong. What I wish to emphasize as my position, however, without desiring to embarrass any one, is this: the Government of Canada, having established the principle of dry 
canteens in this country, ought not tp depart from that principle when our boys go overseas, so long as they are in the training camps. It is idle to say to those of us who live in provinces which have adopted prohibitive legislation that as much liquor is consumed under a dry canteen system as is consumed with the * wet canteen. The greater the number of obstacles thrown in the way of getting liquor, the smaller the consumption will be. I care not whether it is by the authority of the British Government or by the authority of any other Government, this Government is responsible for the welfare of our boys wherever they have control. And in saying this I mean not only the Government, but Parliament. Having made myself clear, let me suggest one other thing.
Tp this Parliament has been entrusted, for five years by the people and for one year by ourselves, the duty of looking after the affairs of Canada whether she be in peace or in war. We cannot escape that responsibility, and we ought to accept the responsibility of discussing these things with each other in a fair way, because it makes no difference whether a man sits on that side or on this side of the House, we are all equally interested, in more ways than one, and we should not fly at each other's heads the minute there is a difference of opinion about these things. I will not quietly allow any member on either side of the House to question my right to discuss the conditions of our Canadian troops either here or in the Motherland. With all due deference to the stirring appeal of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers), I believe our boys at the front look to this Parliament as their guardian (not to any one set of men in it), and any man who hesitates to assume that responsibility, no matter what the criticism, is not performing his full duty. I do not look upon the position of the House of Commons, no matter upon which side we sit, as one that demands silence on these things. If we were all to sit silent, we would soon ascertain that our boys at the front condemned us, believing we were not doing our full duty to them, and no matter what the criticism may be, I believe every member in this House ought to take the situation seriously, and we ought to feel a freedom, particularly in this time of stress through which we are passing, perhaps greater than we ever did before, in pointing out where we can where things may be remedied and efficiency become more efficient. What is Parliament for? Is it for the Government to come in and say: You

must do this and you must do that, and everybody quietly acquiesce? In that case, we might as well all stay at home. Why have a Parliament at all? This is the forum of the people, and if there be any portion of the people of Canada that need protection, need care, need looking after, that portion of the people is to be found in the training camps of the Old Country or fighting for us in France. Surely we are looking at this thing from the wrong angle; we ought to be united as one man in seeing that the very best that can be done for our soldiers at the front is done, and no matter what the views of a man, honestly expressed, may be, the Parliament of Canada is the place in which to express those views.
In conclusion, I want to say again that I am in favour of pursuing this course so long as Canada has control in regard to the canteens, no matter where our boys may be. When they leave the training camps to go into the firing line, I do not intend to set up my opinions against that of those of long experience, but I do say this, that because a man lives in London or elsewhere, he is not a bit better qualified to judge of whether there should be a dry canteen or a wet canteen for the Canadians than we are in this Parliament, and we have said once for all that we are in favour of dry canteens. I am in favour of dry canteens for our boys, no matter whether they be in Canada or in the training camps in the Old Country.

speechtext:
I followed with close attention the speeches delivered in the course of the. debate on this resolution. I have come to the conclusion that far too much significance has been given Mr. Goforth's criticism as expressed in his letter published in the Financial Post. I came across many officers and soldiers who had returned from the front and they were unanimous in the statement that discipline in the camps left nothing to be desired and that they had no trouble whatever from intemperance. The officers stated that in England and France, beer could be had at the canteen after' drill hours, and there is not a man in this House who could find fault with the military authorities for allowing our soldiers to partake of such light refreshments after hours of hard training, just as the French soldier is allowed his glass of wine.
I have just said that we are making too much of Mr. Goforth's letter; the same is true of many other documents that find their way in the public press of this country. This
very afternoon we have had another instance. At the opening of the House, our attention was drawn to a newspaper item alleging that soldiers who cross the province of Quebec are subjected to insults as they march through Montreal, Quebec or Riviere-du-Loup. Whoever is in touch with the prevailing sentiment in the province of Quebec cannot but realize how much it is below the dignity of the House of Commons of Canada to take notice of such abuse, which is launched through the medium of the press by irresponsible parties and is a mere concoction of slanderous untruths. I am quite aware, Mr. Speaker, that if any gentleman this afternoon had moved the adjournment of the House in ordeT to call attention to a statement appearing in a newspaper edited in the province of Ontario suggesting that soldiers had been insulted in the province of Quebec, all my colleagues from our province, standing up in their indignation, would have replied before the House and before the country:	" It is injudicious for us to
take so much stock in a letter published in Ontario or elsewhere on happenings in the province of Quebec." I take this opportunity of .asserting that the criticisms appearing in certain newspapers concerning events alleged to have happened in the province of Quebec are absolutely groundless. Canadian soldiers leaving for the front, from whatever part of the country they hail, are cheered and congratulated as they march through our cities along our country roads. Soane are prone to criticise because in the City of Quebec for instance, the people are not continually displaying their feelings in outward manifestations. If to-day we are less demonstrative, the reason comes not from our lack of interest in the war, but from a peculiarity of human nature. Mr. Speaker, the City of Quebec, einee the month of August 1914, has seen thousands and thousands of soldiers marching past; thirty thousand filed through its gates on their way to Valcartier and later other regiments, going to other camps. So, if the people of the City of Quebec are not on every occasion turning out to give public ovations to our boys parading through the street, does it mean that they are insensible to the sacrifices made by our soldiers? No indeed, Mr. Speaker; heretofore the province of Quebec has been all soul in the war like the rest of the country, and no matter to what extent French Canadians may be belittled in other provinces, they understand their duty and will perform it to the end, and never will they be wanting in admiration not only for our boys from

the province of Quebec, but for every Canadian soldier from any part of the Dominion.
Should we have been justified, Mr. Speaker, to take six hours of the time of this House to discuss the accusations contained in the letter read to us early in the day? Certainly not. And I say we are not justified in spending six hours over what Mr. Goforth may have thought fit to say in his letter. I heard the minister of Labor (Mr. Crothers) giving Mr. Goforth's account of what took place at Valcartier. I was in the City of Quebec in 1914 and every day that our boys were in camp, I made it my duty to go to Valcartier, where I had friends to whom I could be of assistance. In three weeks' time thirty-three thousand men were gathered at that one point. Can it be thought possible that such a large body of men as yet unaccustomed to military discipline, may be collected from every corner of the country without some slight disorders taking place before embarking for the front? Why should those slight disagreements be magnified? Why not, instead, point to the splendid discipline of the troops at Valcartier in 1914, so much admired by all visitors to the camp? The same order prevailed last year. Why be shocked if in a very few cases insignificant breaches of discipline were noticed? Mr. Speaker, there are men right here in Ottawa, a prohibition city, as well as in Montreal and elsewhere, who are not enlisting and nevertheless have their little fling. Should we exhibit unflinching severity on account of 'an occasional infringement of the law by some soldier? I know the members of this House are too broad-minded for such petty criticism.
Hon. gentlemen who have been to the front and have spoken on this question, called attention to the admirable behaviour of all our boys. We all agree that they are well disciplined and made heroes of themselves on the battlefield. I ask whether we who stay behind, and who for the most part lack military training, have the right to say to the military authorities, to say to such a distinguished officer as general Turner, for instance,-a Liberal, by the way

who has charge of the Canadian forces in England, that he does not know what he is about and should in future forbid his men to take a glass of beer. . . Should we dictate to the highest military experts commanding our boys in England and on the Continent? I claim not. As for me, Mr. Speaker, so long as our soldiers, whatever be their nationality, fight >as they fought at Ypres, Langemark, Festubert, Givenchy, and especially Vimy, the military heads who train 
men for such struggles will have my most entire confidence.

I certainly had no intention to delay the business of the House when I brought this question before my fellow-members. I do not regret the course I took, notwithstanding the aspersions and suggestions from the other side, and even from this side. After twenty-one years as a member of this House I know something of my public duty, and, as to loyalty, in that I yield to no one. I did not bring this question forward as suggesting an attack upon the Government, or upon the Minister of Militia and Defence. I made a very mild statement, inspired by a newspaper published in Toronto by a man who is well known to the members of this House and to the community in general, a personal friend of several of the ministers. That newspaper published the letter of Captain Goforth and commented strongly in favour of his attitude. It was my duty as a public man, it was my duty as a friend of the Canadian army in the field, to bring this matter before the House, and I have done it without questioning the bravery, the patriotism, or the fighting qualities of our soldiers. I listened to the speeches that have been delivered in this debate, including that of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers). I can understand a speech of that nature delivered in a back concession by a fifth-grade politician, but when such a speech is delivered in this House by a minister of the Crown it causes me no little surprise. The hon. minister suggested that I should not have spoken at all on this question. Let me tell him that if I had slandered and defamed soldiers I should be in good company, as I will show. But I have not slandered, I have not defamed, I have not libelled our soldiers. Were I to slander and libel them I should slander and libel my own kith and kin. Let me remind my hon. friend, in case he may repeat that address before his electors, that if he ever refers to my statement this afternoon he may tell them that in my family there is one veteran of South Africa, there is one nephew at the front, one nephew killed at Ypres, and my own son is in the army. Therefore, it is as a Canadian, as a loyal subject of His Majesty the King and as the father of a boy Who will soon be at the front that I have spoken this afternoon. I dare say that of these hon. gentlemen 
who have delivered these loyal utterances this afternoon not one of them stated whether he was in favour of a dry or a wet canteen, and not one of them weulu take issue with me if he were standing before his electors. More than that, let me say that I am ready to join issue with any of the hon. gentlemen who have lectured me on loyalty and patriotism not only before this House but in any of their constituencies. I am ready to take the same attitude in front of their own electors-aye, before the Canadian soldiers themselves. I challenge any one to deny me the privilege as a Canadian to speak the language I have spoken this afternoon. The hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) should know that I brought this matter before the House oecau=e I thought it was in the public interest, but he has approached the question in the way which we might expect from a gentleman of his size. Listening to him, when he was suggesting that I had defamed, slandered and libelled the Canadian soldiers, instincts ively I thought of Johnson's definition of a certain loyalty and a certain patriotism.
This is not a political issue in the narrow sense. I claim that this is a national issue. It affects the welfare of our soldiers and of their families. The duty of a public man who happened to possess the information which I imparted to the House this afternoon was to focus the attention of the public on these facts in order to know whether the alleged evil exists or not. What did I say to arouse the anger of my 'hon. friends? I beg each of my hon. friends to read my remarks in tomorrow's Hansard. They will find that first I made the statement that the ex-Minister of Militia had wisely established a dry canteen for the Canadian soldiers. Does anybody take exception to that ? I stated that having establisned a dry canteen, some one whom I do not know had taken it upon himself to substitute wet canteens. In that statement, happily for me, I was corroborated toy the hon. exMinister of Militia himself (Sir Sam Hughes), who stated that he craved the honour of having established the dry canteen, tout that his ex-colleague the Minister of Militia overseas, in order to insult him, had restored the wet canteen in the camps in England. I did not make the statement; the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton made it this afternoon. What did I say further, Mr. Speaker? I said that disorder was alleged to have taken place as a result of the establishment of wet canteens in the camps, and I brought

specific cases to the attention of hon. gentlemen. The Minister of Labour suggested, a few moments ago, that this letter had never been written, that it was not signed, that, indeed, it may have been a forgery. A forgery? The letter is not signed, but on the first line of the first page what do you read, Mr. Speaker?
What the army loses through drink.
By Capt. Paul Goforth.
And my hon. friend thinks it is an argument to state that the letter is not signed after the last line. Mr. Speaker, I stated the specific cases given in that letter by Capt. Goforth, who gives the dates, the circumstances, and the names of the camps. Are the facts true or not? Did I state that they were true? I stated that evils were alleged to exist, that they ought to be investigated, and that if, on investigation, they aTe found to be true, the plain duty of the Minister of Militia is to humbly request the Imperial authorities or the War Office to restore the dry canteen in the camps where our Canadian soldiers are assembled. That is the gist of the remarks I made this afternoon. Why all this anger, why these lessons in loyalty and patriotism? Is the Canadian Parliament afraid to face the issue? Is an issue or a grievance to be settled by discarding it? Either the facts are true or not. If they are not true, so much the worse for Captain Goforth. He is still at the front, and if he has libelled, slandered and defamed his fellow officers and soldiers under him, well, Mr. Speaker, I leave him to the care of his soldiers and his fellow officers. But if they are true, what of it? If the statements contained in Captain Goforth's letters are true, I ask my hon. friend the Minister of Labour will he stand by the wet canteen or will he not stand by the dry canteen?

There is such a thing as compulsory investigation, but I dare say that in the present instance, when statements are made in a respectable and responsible paper like the Financial Post by a friend of the Government, and when the charges of Captain
Goforth are endorsed in a strong editorial, it is the duty of the Government to investigate such charges and find out
10 p.m. if they are true. Every fatheT, every mother, every clergyman, yes, and every respectable citizen in the country will expect that much from the Government.

speechtext: Colonel Maclean, a soldier, holding rank in the Canadian militia, would publish in his paper statements of the nature of a forgery, would defame and slander and libel the four hundred thousand Canadians who are serving abroad? What does my hon. frined think of that?

maintopic: *COMMONS
speechtext: My hon. friend has stated several times that he does not know whether these are facts or not. He admits now he does not know Mr. Goforth or the editor of the paper.

maintopic: *COMMONS
speechtext: The House will surely not expect that I shall answer the interjection of my hon. friend. I say that according to Captain Goforth, who is still in the army, who therefore comes under discipline, disorders of a very serious nature have taken place and those disorders are enumerated by the Financial Post published by Colonel Maclean of Toronto, a supporter of the Government, a friend of the Minister of Finance. Mr. Speaker, if the alleged facts which I have mentioned are untrue, we have a board of censors in Canada. Why not suspend the publication of the Financial Post? If the statements by Captain Goforth, which I have quoted, are not facts, why not cashier him at once? But no, the Minister of Labour would like the member for Rouville to investigate the facts beforehand.

The member for Huron (Mr. Lewis) spoke of his experience and stated that drunkenness in the army in England was an unpardonable sin, and that anyone guilty of drunkenness was court martialled. Exactly; and I find that Captain Goforth speaks of such a case. He says:
Soon after our arrival at Shorncliffe there was a special meeting' of the officers' mess to decide whether we would go on with a "wet" mess or follow the example of Lord Kitchener and the King-
A disloyal Kitchener and a disloyal King I suppose.
Broadminded arguments about "liberty" and "moderation'' won the day. Yet, within a month from that time, X had the unwelcome task-	.
Mr. Speaker, mark my words.
Yet, within a month from that time, I had the unwelcome task of prosecuting two of my brother officers for drunkenness before a General Court Martial, and our Regimental Sergeant-Major for Ithe same offence before a District Court Martial. The Sergeant-Major was found guilty of drunkenness at Hythe on the line of march and was dismissed from the service. He appealed to the Privy Council, but the judgment of the court was sustained. There was a man who knew his work to perfection, who had served in the South African war, and who wore on his breast the ribbon of the long service and good conduct medal; and yet he was broken completely, and broken through nothing but drink. Why should' a capable warrant officer be dismissed from the service? Why should an efficient officer be cashiered? Is it not high time that we determined to dismiss the liquor traffic from the service? Is it not the liquor traffic that should be cashiered?
That is the language of an officer in His Majesty's army, a Canadian, and yet, because I report to the House that serious state of things, I am told that I should have kept silent, that I should not have even mooted the subject before the House this afternoon. I repeat that I have done only my duty. Now I am told by the member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury), who lost his temper, that this Captain Goforth is nothing else but a crank. Well, if Captain Goforth is a crank, it is a very serious aspersion on the Minister of Militia and the military authorities generally who have sent our boys under fire commanded by a crank. That is not a certificate of very great wisdom on the part of the military authorities.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance also stated that it was a slander to mention such facts, a slander against our soldiers at the front. I do not know if he listened

to my statements this afternoon, but if his accusation of slander is based on hearsay,
I would tell him that the hearsay comes from warped and twisted interpretations of my statements. I simply enumerated the various statements made by Captain Goforth, and the mere stating of these allegations should not bring on my head the thunder which was brought this afternoon. As I stated a moment ago, if I have slandered the soldiers I am in good company, because in England, in the British Parliament, the mother of all Parliaments, the Prime Minister was not afraid to tackle the problem of liquor in the army. I have his very words here, delivered a few months ago. He said:
We are fighting Germany, Austria, and drink, and so far as I can see the greatest of these deadly foes Is drink.
Is Lloyd -George a libeller? Is he a slanderer? Is he disloyal? Surely not, since he is at the head of the present Government. If he were disloyal he would be in excellent company with Rt. Hon. Walter Long, Lord Milner, Rt. Hon. Bonar Law and all the other leaders of the Tory party in England. . Mr. Speaker, no, it is the duty of a member who has the interest of his fellow citizens at heart, to bring to light facts such as I have revealed to-day. I resent more especially the remarks which were made by my friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark). I regret that he is not in his seat at the present moment. He thinks that because the Empire is at war, and because Canada is at war, we should maintain silence and not divulge abuses and weaknesses such as are set forth in the statement made by Captain Goforth. Of course, if there was no war there would be no soldiers and no camps, and if there were no camps there would be no wet canteens and therefore " there would be no disorders and we would have nothing to say. But unfortunately there is war and, as I said a moment ago, it is not by ignoring a grievance which exists that you settle it. The hon. member for Red Deer claims to he and is an excellent Liberal. As a Liberal of the English school I believe that, after all, the cure for all evils is publicity. My hon. friend lectured me with regard to the -soldiers fighting in the trenches. Did I speak of the trenches? The only reference I made to the trenches was when I said that the Russian Government, having sent soldiers to France, had exacted from the French military authorities an agreement that in the trenches where the

French soldiers were served wine the Russian soldiers should not receive any liquor at the hands of their Allies. My hon. friend hinted that I had spoken with spme disparagement of the work done in the trenches. He spoke of Verdun and of the heroic battles in which the French soldiers were engaged. I did not need that lecture, for I know what the French soldiers have accomplished just as well as I know what the English and the Canadian soldiers have accomplished at the fr.ont. I do not begrudge the small rum ration which is served to our soldiers in the mud of the trenches. I did not speak of that: I spoke of the life of the soldiers at the camps in England. I said that it was alleged that the wet canteens at these camps had been the cause of innumerable disorders and I pleaded that the Government take action to restore the dry canteen and to make representations to the Imperial authorities to that end. If my hon. friend from Red Deer were in his seat, I would remind him that it i.s the essence of Liberalism to expose evils in order to free society from their effects. Describing the aim of Liberalism, Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman said:
We would endeavour to secure to every man the best conditions of living-, and so far as can be done by laws and customs, to secure him also an equal chance with others of a useful and happy life.
Lord Willoughby de Broke has said:
The essence of our policy is to give each individual the elements that will afford him an opportunity of at least living a free and a decorous existence, and the opportunity to raise himself or herself to the highest point of moral and material efficiency.
I say that it is the act of a true Liberal to ask for the suppression of intoxicants in the training camps, because liquor does not make for the moral or material efficiency of the soldier. My hon. friend, I know, has three sons at the front. I have only one who will be at the front very soon, and I would rather have my son live in a camp under respectable conditions than have him exposed to the temptations to which our soldiers are constantly subjected because of intoxicants. Mr. Speaker, I beg to withdraw the motion that I made this afternoon.
Motion of Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux for the adjournment of the House negatived.
On motion of Sir Thomas White, the House adjourned at 10.24 p.m.
Friday, April 27, 1917.
